title: Inclusion is Not a Room
author: Nickhart, Mr.
summary: Both the UK government and the UAE’s KHDA have been clear about what inclusion means. The Dubai Inclusive Education Policy Framework defines it as educating all students in a common learning environment, one where all students have access to quality instruction, intervention and support and where they become fully participating members of the learning community. The UK’s 2026 Schools White Paper commits to a mainstream system where most children with additional needs are supported effectively alongside their peers, underpinned by new National Inclusion Standards and a statutory duty on every school to publish an inclusion strategy. The white paper commits GBP3bn to create 50,000 new inclusion base places in mainstream schools, with an expectation that every secondary, and an equivalent number of primary places, will have a dedicated space for specialist teaching or targeted support. The DfE’s inclusion bases guidance , published this month, sets out what that investment is expected to produce. In Dubai, many schools already have significant inclusion departments with specialisms on site. The question both systems are now facing is the same one. Share with a colleague who cares about inclusion: The KHDA framework defines the barriers to inclusion as attitudes, beliefs, practices, physical or technological obstacles, or the lack of support, that result in a student’s exclusion from, or in their less-than-full participation as a valued equal in, the common learning environment. The DfE guidance frames it the same way. That definition locates the problem not in the child but in the school. The barrier is not the student’s diagnosis. It is the attitude, the practice, or the absence of support that prevents full participation. One student, two inclusion base experiences What the DfE calls the continuum model plays out in practice something like this. An inclusion room can be a barrier. It can also reduce them. The difference is entirely in how school leaders position it. Here is how a room becomes a barrier: A student who finds the mainstream classroom overwhelming is sent to the inclusion base. Staff report that they are calmer there. The student requests to go there. Over time, their timetable drifts towards more time in the base and less time in class. The inclusion base becomes their unofficial primary educational environment. They have fewer relationships and shared curriculum experiences with peers. Their progress diverges from that of their year group. And the school, at every step, has acted with kindness. This is what the non-example separation from peers or over-reliance on adult support actually looks like in practice. It might not have had a decision moment. It probably happened over many moments of intense emotion and immediate responses to need or safety, each of which is defensible in the moment. Here is how a room reduces a barrier. A student who finds the mainstream classroom overwhelming is identified early. The school maps the specific moments that are hardest (transitions between subjects, unstructured time, lessons with high ambient noise). Rather than sending the student to the inclusion base when things become difficult, the school uses the base proactively: a fifteen-minute settling period at the start of the day with a trusted adult, and a quick but purposeful debrief after lunch before afternoon lessons begin. In class, the teacher has made specific adjustments: seating, predictable routines, pre-teaching of lesson content that reduce the number of moments that feel unmanageable. The base is used to build regulatory capacity, not to provide refuge from a classroom that hasn’t changed. There is a clear record of when the student accesses the base, why, and what the intended outcome is. The support plan names what success looks like, not ’calmer in the base’ but ’able to remain in class for extended periods without distress’. The student is involved in reviewing whether that is happening. There is a plan for what it would look like to need the base less. Six weeks in, the morning settling session has reduced from fifteen minutes to ten. The goal is visible, the direction is clear and the mainstream classroom remains the student’s primary environment. The student in this example and the student in the first one may present identically on a Tuesday afternoon. The difference is not in the child. It is in whether the school has a belief, a plan and the discipline to use the room in service of both.
